issues.description: HAS_NAMED regex includes numeric keywords like 'bolder'/'lighter' but also risks matching substrings inside identifiers without /i applied symmetrically to HAS_NUMERIC.
issues.detail: HAS_NAMED uses /i and \b, but \b in JS regex treats digits as word chars. So HAS_NUMERIC=/\b(?:100|200|...|900)\b/ will match '100' inside '1000' only at boundary — correct — but will also match the literal '400' inside CSS custom property names like '--weight-400'. State the invariant: 'value contains a numeric font-weight token outside identifiers.' A var() reference like var(--w400) would trigger a false positive bypass-skip; verify or document.

issues.description: import-notation 'url' fast-path skips when params contain 'url(' anywhere, including inside strings/comments.
issues.detail: The check /url\(/i.test(params) returns early when primary==='url' if the substring appears. But '@import "foo-url(bar).css"' contains 'url(' inside a string and is actually a string-notation import. The fast-skip would incorrectly suppress the diagnostic. Invariant should be 'params parses to a url() function node,' not 'substring url( appears.' Recommend a tighter test or anchor to leading token.

issues.description: keyframe HAS_PERCENTAGE regex omits the /i flag, so 'FROM'/'TO' uppercase keywords are not caught when primary==='keyword'.
issues.detail: HAS_KEYWORD has /i but HAS_PERCENTAGE does not. PERCENTAGE_SELECTORS likely contains '0%','100%','from','to' — and CSS is case-insensitive for keyframe keywords. Wait: primary==='keyword' uses HAS_PERCENTAGE to detect percentages-to-flag. Percentages have no case, so /i is moot there. However selectorRegex=/./ for the third branch always matches, which is fine. State the invariant for the reader in a comment; right now the three-way assignment lacks explanation.

issues.description: selector-pseudo-element-colon-notation walkRules(/:/) matches any colon, including attribute selectors like [href="a:b"].
issues.detail: The previous code did ruleNode.selector.includes(':') which has the same imprecision, so behavior is preserved — the fast-path is no worse. But the regex /:/ applied by postcss walkRules tests against the selector string, so attribute selectors with quoted colons still pass through to parseSelector. Acceptable as a coarse prefilter; the invariant 'selector text contains a colon' is correct for a superset filter. Add a one-line comment naming it as such.

issues.description: Performance claim is unmeasured in the PR; no benchmark numbers accompany the 'Fix performance' title.
issues.detail: The change is plausibly a real speedup (early-exit before invoking valueParser/parseSelector on the common case). But the PR contains no profile, no before/after timings, no microbenchmark. The optimization is in the critical 3% for standard-config rules walking every decl/rule, so it likely is worth doing — but the discipline is: measure. Request a benchmark line in the changeset or a linked profile to justify the added regex compilation and call-site complexity.

issues.description: Three new module-level RegExp objects are constructed from imported keyword sets at import time without literate comment.
issues.detail: HAS_NAMED, HAS_NUMERIC, HAS_PERCENTAGE, HAS_KEYWORD are compiled once per module load — correct choice, avoids re-compilation per decl. But a future reader sees `new RegExp(\\b(?:${[...].join('|')})\\b, 'i')` with no comment stating 'fast-path prefilter: superset of values that could violate primary option X; false positives fall through to the parser, false negatives would be bugs.' Add that one comment block; it converts these from clever code into literate code.

review.summary: UNDER-AUDITED on two fronts: the fast-path regex prefilters look correct as supersets but the invariant 'a positive match here means the value *might* violate primary; a negative match guarantees it cannot' is nowhere stated in code or PR. Two prefilters have asymmetric semantics worth verifying: HAS_NUMERIC will match digits inside identifiers/custom-properties, and import-notation's /url\\(/i matches the substring inside strings. The performance claim is unmeasured — likely real (these rules ship in the standard config and walk every decl) but the discipline is to attach a number. Recommend: add literate comments naming each regex as a 'superset prefilter,' tighten import-notation's url() detection, and include a one-line benchmark result in the changeset.
